title: Ezekiel 8:14–18
context: Ezekiel 8:14–18 completes the tour of abominations, still in the prophet’s voice with the LORD speaking to him. At the north gate of the LORD’s house women sit weeping for Tammuz (8:14). Tammuz is a deity mourned in the ancient Near East; further details of the background are debated, and these notes do not press them. In the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men stand with their backs toward the LORD’s temple and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun (8:16; compare Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 23:5, 11). The place between the porch and the altar is where Joel 2:17 calls the priests to “weep between the porch and the altar”, named here without harmonizing; readers differ on whether the twenty-five are priests, and they are not necessarily the twenty-five men of 11:1. The LORD says the people have filled the land with violence and provoked him, and adds, “Behold, they put the branch to their nose.” (8:17). The meaning of this gesture is uncertain; suggestions include a ritual act connected with the worship just described or an insulting gesture, and no single explanation is settled. The LORD then says he will deal in wrath, will not spare or pity, and will not hear their cry (8:18). Both traditions read the passage soberly as shared ground, holding that worship turned from the LORD to created things, joined with violence, brings judgment.

verses.text: Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the LORD’s house which was toward the north; and I saw the women sit there weeping for Tammuz.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD brings Ezekiel to the north gate of the LORD’s house, where women sit weeping for Tammuz. Arminian readers note that Tammuz is a deity mourned in the ancient Near East, and they read the scene soberly as worship directed to another god at the very gate of the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the background of Tammuz loosely and do not press details beyond the text. They read the scene as showing that the abominations reached every part of the community, and they treat the passage as shared ground on the LORD’s judgment of idolatry.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Have you seen this, son of man? You will again see yet greater abominations than these.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Have you seen this, son of man? You will again see yet greater abominations than these.” Arminian readers note the question invites the prophet to grasp the seriousness of what he has seen, and they see the coming scene as the most offensive of all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same question and read the repeated pattern as the LORD’s careful presentation of evidence before judgment. They observe that the prophet is not left to interpret alone but is guided by God’s questions, a feature both traditions read as shared ground.

verses.text: He brought me into the inner court of the LORD’s house; and I saw at the door of the LORD’s temple, between the porch and the altar, there were about twenty-five men with their backs toward the LORD’s temple and their faces toward the east. They were worshiping the sun toward the east.
verses.arminianNotes: In the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men stood with their backs toward the LORD’s temple, worshiping the sun toward the east. Arminian readers note the vivid picture of turning one’s back on God, and they compare Deuteronomy 4:19 and 2 Kings 23:5, 11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and observe that the place between the porch and the altar is where Joel 2:17 calls the priests to weep, named without harmonizing. They hold open whether these men are priests, and they read the scene as shared ground on idolatry at the center of worship.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Have you seen this, son of man? Is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they commit the abominations which they commit here? For they have filled the land with violence, and have turned again to provoke me to anger. Behold, they put the branch to their nose.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether it is a light thing that Judah commits these abominations, fills the land with violence, and provokes him, adding, “Behold, they put the branch to their nose.” Arminian readers note that the meaning of the gesture is uncertain and they do not press any single explanation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the gesture is obscure, with suggestions including a ritual act or an insulting gesture, and they leave it unresolved. They observe that the LORD joins violence with idolatry, and both traditions read the verse as showing that false worship and injustice go together.

verses.text: Therefore I will also deal in wrath. My eye won’t spare, neither will I have pity. Though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, yet I will not hear them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Therefore I will also deal in wrath. My eye won’t spare, neither will I have pity.” Arminian readers note the severity of the announcement and read it as the response to long and persistent rebellion, set within a book that also holds out the LORD’s later restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same severity and read it as the just sentence on a people who have turned from God. They observe that the refusal to hear their cry marks a point of judgment in the vision, and both traditions read it soberly without making it the whole of the book’s message.
